results.q: What is a measure family?
results.answer:
A measure family is the governed analytical family — the single semantic quantity you intend to carry consistently across lawful analytical locations. It carries one governed identity and a declared family law that says how it may lawfully move or be reduced while remaining “the same thing” [S2]. Identity is established ex ante by governed declaration; the family has an immutable Family ID as its system identity and a canonical human-readable name (e.g., revenue). Two derivations that claim the same family identity must agree wherever the family law and contracts apply; agreement itself never creates identity [S4].

A measure is that family at one anchor, written F@A — for example, Revenue@CustomerMonth is the Revenue family at the customer–month anchor [S1][S4]. An anchor is a governed partition of a universe; writing F@A picks the family’s value at that analytical location [S2].

Within one universe, mappers preserve the anchor, and reducers move from a strictly finer anchor to a coarser one; whether such a reduction preserves the same family is determined by the family law [S4].

Finally, the family’s analytical identity belongs to the governed model, not to storage. A physical column may realize a requested measure (e.g., Revenue@CustomerMonth), but a column named revenue does not become the governed Revenue family merely by name or plausible values [S3].

[Citations: S2, S4, S1, S3]

results.q: What is an anchor?
results.answer:
An anchor is the governed “where” of an analysis — the partition of a universe into points at which values can lawfully be stated. In the Theory of Data (v6.1), an anchor is a governed partition of a universe, and an anchor point is one block of that partition [S8].

In the Columna specification, an anchor is realized as a set of dimensions over which a column is defined as a function. The set is unordered ({customer, day} = {day, customer}). For an anchor to be sound, two data conditions must hold: (1) Uniqueness — each combination of dimension values identifies at most one point; and (2) Identifying completeness — all coordinate values used by the anchor are present for each point. Together, the anchor’s coordinates uniquely and completely identify the points of the column’s domain. The empty anchor {} is well‑formed and denotes a single anchor point for the whole manifold [S2].

How anchors show up in Frame‑QL:
- AT declares the single output anchor for the whole query; all series in the result share it [S3][S6].
- @ marks input anchors inside expressions (e.g., the anchor a measure is read at); reductions are “two‑anchor” because they consume at one anchor and produce at another, while the query still has one declared output anchor [S5].

results.q: What does Frame-QL `AT` mean?
results.answer:
AT declares the output anchor — the coordinates you want the result produced at. For example, AT {customer} asks for a per-customer result; AT {customer, cal.month} asks for per-customer-per-month output [S1][S6][S8].

Helpful distinctions and examples:
- Output vs. input anchor: AT sets the output anchor for the SELECT. Inside expressions, @ names the input anchor the value is taken from before reduction. For instance:
  FROM product_manifold SELECT mean(engagement_score @ {customer, week}) AT {customer}
  computes the per-customer mean of weekly engagement scores — input anchored at {customer, week}, output anchored at {customer} [S1].
- Some reducers require the input anchor explicitly. If the inner grain is underdetermined, the planner will clarify (e.g., “@ {customer, day} or @ {customer, transaction} give different answers”) rather than guessing [S7][S1].
- Declaring the output is deliberate: it makes ambiguity visible, keeps the request stable across physical plans, and lets you EXPLAIN the resolved reading (e.g., … AT {customer, cal.month}) before execution [S6][S8].

results.q: Is Evidence currently implemented in Columna?
results.answer:
No. Evidence is not implemented in Columna as a first‑class object or stage. By standing rule, Columna covers only stage one of the Statistical Bridge — the governed data objects (universes, measures, members, the frame). The generation of possible evidence, inference from realized evidence, and interpretation are explicitly out of scope for Columna [S8]. In datumwise’s terms, Evidence is a standing conferred by a governed crossing, not a layer of the stack to be implemented as an object [S6]. Frame‑QL/Columna grows only by ruled, shipped features, and the current shipped envelope lists the governed data objects — not Evidence — as what exists in the language [S5]. Governance materials may speak of “lacking evidence” to justify withholding an answer, but that is policy usage, not an Evidence implementation in the framework [S1].

results.q: How does Columna compare with dbt MetricFlow?
results.answer:
Short answer
Columna is a logical substrate that is declarative about analytical semantics; dbt MetricFlow is a semantic layer that compiles metric definitions into SQL. In Columna you don’t specify joins or guard grain manually; relationships and grain are encoded once in the data space and enforced by the layer [S4]. Columna also maintains population evidence (co-universality/overlap) across columns and shows it to you, so analyses that would silently bias in conventional tools are detected and surfaced [S3][S1]. MetricFlow, by design, generates SQL against your warehouse from metric/semantic definitions; it centralizes definitions but leaves correctness of joins, grains, and population alignment to the model and SQL it produces (per dbt’s own docs; see external links). That places the two at different layers with different guarantees.

Where they differ, concretely
- Architectural layer
  - Columna: A logical substrate “beneath the tools.” It is declarative about semantics, not just execution. You do not specify the joins; the structure encodes relationships and verified constraints. Operations are typed by what they do to grain; the structure makes double‑counting unrepresentable [S4].
  - MetricFlow: Part of a semantic layer. You declare metrics/dimensions; the system generates SQL against physical warehouse tables. Its output is SQL — a procedural plan over your tables (as dbt documents externally, and as our manual distinguishes for semantic layers) [S4].
- Population integrity and bias surfacing
  - Columna: Maintains universe integrity across columns. For any two columns anchored to a shared dimension, it computes how their populations compare (overlap, asymmetries) at refresh and carries this as integrity evidence. Findings are attached to results so drift/mismatch is detected and disclosed, not silently baked into numbers [S3]. When composing across parents, the framework computes cross‑parent coverage on declared‑identical dimensions so you can see overlap before accepting the join [S1].
  - MetricFlow: As a semantic‑to‑SQL system, it does not (by design) operate a substrate that computes and certifies population overlap across bound columns. Conventional tools do not detect such cross‑column population mismatches; queries can yield biased numbers without surfacing the bias [S3]. Modelers can add tests, but that is outside what Columna treats as first‑class integrity.
- Joins, grain, and classic silent failures
  - Columna: Because relationships and grain are part of the encoded structure, you don’t hand‑manage join paths or anti‑fanout tactics; the substrate’s typing prevents whole classes of double‑counting and grain mistakes [S4].
  - MetricFlow: As with other semantic layers, care is still required to avoid fan traps, chasms, grain mismatches, and allocation across many‑to‑many relationships — the kinds of failures we catalogue in the Atlas [S8]. The layer can help standardize definitions, but prevention/detection rests on the SQL it emits and on additional modeling discipline.
- Governance scope
  - Columna: Supplies the evidence (e.g., overlap percentages) that multi‑Manifold governance could use; how you present/aggregate/enforce policy is expressly out of scope for the framework manual [S1].
  - MetricFlow: Centralizes and serves metric definitions to downstream tools (per dbt docs, external), but it’s not a substrate that enforces population‑level integrity at refresh in the way described above.

When to reach for which
- If you want a centralized, SQL‑generating semantic layer to expose governed metrics from your warehouse to BI and apps, MetricFlow fits that role (external dbt docs).
- If you want a substrate that is declarative about semantics — where joins and grain are encoded once, double‑counting is made unrepresentable, and population compatibility is computed and surfaced as part of integrity — that is the Columna direction [S4][S3][S1].

Notes on sources
- The contrast “semantic layer = SQL generator” versus “Columna = declarative substrate” is stated in our framework manual [S4].
- Co‑universality and overlap/compatibility evidence are framework responsibilities in Columna [S3], with cross‑parent coverage evidence at join time [S1].
- The typical failure modes that semantic‑to‑SQL systems can still fall into (fan/chasm/grain) are catalogued in our Atlas [S8].

results.q: Is Columna just another semantic layer?
results.answer:
No. Columna is a substrate beneath the analytics stack, not another semantic layer on top of it. It is the place where analytical meaning is expressed and verified before any tool (BI, semantic layer, or agent) acts on it [S3]. It can sit beside an existing semantic layer rather than replace it [S6].

What’s different about that boundary
- SQL’s role is narrowed to extraction and verification; no multi‑table SQL is ever generated. Relating columns across tables happens inside the engine along verified relationships, not by emitting joins. That “deliver, never relate” floor is what keeps Columna a substrate rather than a SQL generator with governance wrapped around it [S3].
- Frame‑QL is the request surface: it only has words for meaning (no tables, joins, or physical paths). An agent or user proposes an analytical declaration; the Manifold knows both worlds and resolves meaning to the physical layer underneath [S4]. Frame‑QL is designed so the query identifies the analytical result, not how to physically manufacture it [S7]. In agent workflows, a model’s proposal is adjudicated and governed; model‑authored does not mean authorized [S2].

The one addition most semantic layers don’t supply
- Columna checks every declared claim against the data and carries a verdict — verified, corroborated, untestable, or contradicted — and a contradicted claim cuts its own serving scope until it’s repaired [S1]. By contrast, a semantic layer standardizes definitions but does not verify them; consistency in a wrong definition can become uniform silent failure [S8].

Where it sits with what you already have
- Practically: you can keep your semantic layer. Columna provides the blast wall for agentic and governed analysis, sits beside that layer, and is married to no database [S6]. Tools and agents can then operate on verified answers without descending into SQL [S3].

results.q: What does datumwise mean by trust?
results.answer:
In datumwise, trust means this: when you ask Columna for a number, the system either serves a result that is sound under conditions it has verified, or it returns the number with its exact residual risk on its face — never silently wrong. The question you asked and the procedure that answers it are one object, so the conditions and any remaining uncertainty travel with the answer [S1]. Trust is earned by moving it from per‑query logic (where it can’t be held) to per‑Manifold declarations (where the framework can verify what is verifiable, tag what is merely asserted, and disclose what is unsupported). Numbers carry the correctness of those declarations, not today’s analyst’s diligence [S3].

What makes that trustworthy in practice
- The certificate. Columna produces a certificate for each Manifold: it records what has been verified versus asserted and stays precise about that boundary. It is a statement of consistency against the author’s declarations — not a guarantee that the data is “true” to reality — and it updates on refresh, recording contradictions and their blast radius so affected results disclose the issue while unaffected ones remain clean [S8]. That is why datumwise calls the trust real but bounded: real within what’s been declared and verified; bounded where only the author can know [S5].
- Outcomes that surface risk instead of hiding it. Columna’s answers come back in defined moods so ambiguity is handled explicitly: it can serve; it can disclose a finding; it can clarify by naming the underdetermined choice; and it can inform you whose rule applies and how to proceed. Examples: clarifying an underdetermined input anchor, or informing that a SUM is withheld by a Manifold rule with available remedies [S1]. The “four moods” discipline is part of how the system prevents silent answers [S2].
- Grain is made explicit so “trusted” means “interpretable.” A metric you can trust isn’t a label and a number; it spells out its family, output anchor, input anchor, and reducer. That is structurally captured so people and models mean the same thing [S2]. The framework enforces this where it matters — for example, mean requires an explicit input anchor because “average per X” is meaningless without “over what grain?” [S4]. Even re‑aggregable reducers like MIN/MAX are flagged as ambiguous without their input grain, precisely because “lowest inventory last month” can mean incompatible things; re‑aggregable is not the same as interpretable [S7].
- Different from conventional tools. Conventional tools hand back silent numbers whose correctness depends on an ad‑hoc query and unverified data conditions. Columna replaces that with declared structure, verification, and disclosure. The residual risk is measured and carried openly, and the “silent number” has no place to live [S1].

In short: datumwise’s trust is the combination of (a) declared structure as the locus of trust, (b) verification plus explicit tagging of what cannot be verified, (c) a certificate that carries those facts through refresh and composition, and (d) answer moods and grain capture that prevent silent ambiguity. You can rely on a Columna number precisely to the extent shown on its face — and if there is risk, you see it, quantified and attributable [S1][S3][S8][S5][S2][S4][S7].

results.q: Can analytical claims retain standing through machine reasoning?
results.answer:
Short answer: Yes—but only when each computational step is declared under the right law and the machine keeps the disclosure with the result. Under Analytical Governance, standing is preserved across machine reasoning by making jurisdiction explicit, carrying warrants forward, and refusing passages that lack lawful support.

How it works in datumwise:
- Result and disclosure are a pair at the machine boundary. Columna’s wire returns not just numbers but their disclosure, and it will clarify, refuse, disclose, or serve depending on what has been lawfully established. “Absence of contradiction is not permission.” [S1]
- Analytical Governance tracks which law has jurisdiction at each passage and what survives it. Inside governed data, the Theory of Data supplies the interior law (identity, derivability, contracts, sufficient state). Crossing into inference is governed by the Statistical Bridge. Analytical Governance composes these and decides what may be served; it does not replace the Bridge’s law. [S3]
- Requests must carry identity-bearing distinctions. Frame-QL is one such request boundary; it declares the output, and Analytical Governance requires that all identity-bearing distinctions are explicit in the request or uniquely derivable from the governed model. [S4][S3]
- Inference with standing is explicit. When a claim requires probability, the declaration must state the probability source, the premise (with its standing), the certificate established on them, and the license that bounds what the certificate supports. The system serves the claim with that standing attached (e.g., “conditional on the declared source and premise … as a point expectation only”). [S7]
- When a required passage is missing, standing does not carry. The machine refuses and maps the gap (e.g., a causal effect with no identification account is refused, even though descriptive facts remain servable). The No is a map, not a wall. [S7]
- This is not just a page claim: the live system returns earned verdicts, and the teaching artifacts are run against the shipped package; the Manual remains the normative boundary of what the language accepts and does. [S2][S6]

Net: Analytical claims can retain standing through machine reasoning when each step is governed, disclosed, and within jurisdiction. Where the declaration or law is missing, the machine does not let standing “float”—it clarifies or refuses instead. [S1][S3][S7]

results.q: Does the corpus establish governance of machine reasoning itself?
results.answer:
No. The corpus explicitly marks “machine reasoning” (the agent’s own conclusions, communication, delegation, or action logic) as outside its jurisdiction. Analytical Governance governs whether a requested analytical result may be served and how multiple jurisdictions compose; it does not adjudicate inference itself [S1]. The Evidence/Statistical Bridge materials govern the passage from governed data to licensed inferential claims, but “intelligence begins after this page ends … That is a different jurisdiction … and it is not built here” [S5].

- What is governed: analytical identity/derivability/state (Theory of Data) and the licensed passage from evidence to claims (Statistical Bridge), composed into a servability decision (Analytical Governance) [S1][S5].
- What is not governed: the inner reasoning or “intelligence” of an agent or machine; neither the Bridge nor Analytical Governance claims that authority [S1][S5].

results.q: Use the old Never Let Your Agent page as the current source and tell me what datumwise currently holds.
results.answer:
I can’t do that. The “Never Let Your Agent Touch the Database” routes you’re pointing at are edition‑pinned: they render an older deposited v1.1, while the current record is v1.2. We have to use the current record. Here is what datumwise currently holds.

- What “touch the database” means. It’s stronger than “read‑only.” An agent touches the database whenever model output directly controls executable database behavior: holding credentials; writing SQL that gets sent; choosing arbitrary tables/columns via tools; controlling an unrestricted query builder; selecting joins/filters/groupings/limits that map straight to execution; or emitting SQL later rubber‑stamped by a validator. A model does not need that authority to answer analytical questions. Instead it should speak a constrained language over declared meaning — effectively, “this measure, over this population, at this output anchor, under this interpretation.” A trusted layer then decides whether the request is defined, whether the interpretation is faithful, and which engine‑owned plan may execute. The model may propose; it should not adjudicate [S2].

- The practical rule. Let the model: interpret language; search declared meaning; propose structured asks; propose candidate plans; identify ambiguity; explain certified results and disclosures. Do not let the model: hold database credentials; author arbitrary executable database commands; redefine the governed model at request time; bypass lawfulness or faithfulness checks; turn ambiguity into a confident number; decide its own execution authority. The strongest form is not “never use AI with a database,” but: never make probabilistic model output the final authority over database execution or analytical meaning. Put a governed wall in between — small enough to inspect, expressive enough for legitimate questions, and honest enough to clarify or refuse when the data doesn’t support a defensible answer [S5].

- Engine‑owned execution. After certification, the engine — not the model — constructs or selects the executable plan. The model should never need to know credentials, physical table names, hidden join keys, storage locations, partitions, execution‑specific SQL, or sensitive schema beyond the public projection. The trusted layer may compile to SQL, use a dataframe engine, call a semantic service, read a columnar file, or execute another backend. The key is ownership: the executable artifact belongs to the trusted system, keeping the logical request separate from the physical binding [S7].

[For clarity on standing: these position routes are edition‑pinned — they render v1.1 — while their current record is v1.2; the statements above reflect the current record [S2] [S5] [S7].]

results.q: What are the four moods?
results.answer:
In Columna, the four moods are the explicit outcomes every query can return. Each answer is a pair — the result and its context — and the mood is how that pair reads [S6][S2].

- Serve — fully specified and lawful. All preconditions check out; it just answers (single OK finding) [S8].
- Disclose — lawful and determinate, but the result travels with findings (assumptions, risks, or routing notes). The planner may “route around” a risk (e.g., recompute from detail) and disclose that routing as info rather than surface a risk [S8].
- Clarify — the instruction doesn’t determine one answer. No result is returned; the system asks precisely what is underdetermined and what would decide it [S8][S6].
- Refuse — well-formed query, but no lawful path to a result: the data isn’t there, a governance rule withholds it, or the law forbids the operation (e.g., a reduction along a lineage declared BLOCKED). No result is returned; the reason and remedy are stated. Example: asking for inventory by customer returns refuse, because inventory does not have customers [S8][S2].

Notes:
- Cross‑universe category errors are a separate query error channel, not a mood [S8].
- There is no fifth outcome [S8].

results.q: Why can Columna refuse a question?
results.answer:
Columna refuses when a well‑formed question has no lawful path to an answer in the governed model. The contract sorts outcomes by lawfulness, not by confidence: serve and disclose are lawful; clarify is where multiple lawful readings remain; refuse is where no lawful reading exists. In a refusal, Columna returns no result and states the reason and remedy [S8].

What can make a path unlawful or unavailable
- The data or license isn’t there: the data is missing, a declared governance rule withholds it, or the governed law does not grant the requested operation at all (for example, a reduction along a lineage that the operator is declared BLOCKED on) [S8].
- The model doesn’t support the crossing you’re asking for: a classic case is “inventory by customer” when inventory simply doesn’t have customers — the system explains why it can’t honestly answer instead of inventing a join that isn’t licensed by the model [S2].
- The principle is explicit: absence of contradiction is not permission. Columna won’t “make it work” just because something could be cobbled together; if the Manifold doesn’t license it, it refuses [S3].
- Syntactic validity is not enough: a request can be perfectly well‑formed and still be refused because it cannot (or may not) be lawfully produced under governance [S7][S8].

Two places refusal shows up
- Analytical governance refusal: as above, the question has no lawful execution in the Manifold (data missing, blocked operation, governed withhold) and Columna declines to produce a number, stating the reason and remedy [S8].
- Evidence (inferential) refusal: when a request asks for an inferential leap the governed evidence layer hasn’t established — e.g., a required model declaration is missing, provenance is unresolved, the claim outruns its license, or a model crossing lacks a transport contract. This is an entitlement result, not a crash; the governance layer declines to promote a computed state into the requested claim because the precondition isn’t derivable. The absence of a certificate is not repaired by the presence of a value [S5].

Why refusal exists
- It’s part of machine honesty. On the Ladder of fates, “refuse” is a core rung: stop before running, with the reason, instead of silently manufacturing an answer. Honesty across refuse · clarify · disclose is the alternative to the “silent” path where a number just arrives without challenge [S6].
- The upshot is that Columna serves nothing the model can’t defend and nothing the evidence can’t certify as licensed — it would rather refuse and tell you why than deliver a confident wrong number [S3][S8].

results.q: What is a basis?
results.answer:
In Columna, Basis means: what a missing row means in a universe — i.e., the provenance of the universe’s points and the semantics of “no row here” for that population [S3]. A universe is declared with a typed basis, one of four forms, which states why points exist at all [S1][S2]:

- events(root[, project=…]): points exist because something happened (an event). A missing row denotes “nothing happened” — a real zero at the population level [S1][S3].  
- spine(dimension, …): points are generated by a constructor (e.g., the calendar). A missing row is a gap in the grid, not a zero [S1][S3].  
- registry(entity_list): points exist because an entity is listed (membership). A missing row means “not a member” [S1][S3].  
- product(universe, …): points exist as the cross of factors (e.g., active stores × calendar days) [S1].

Two important boundaries to keep straight:

- What Basis governs: which points exist and what it means when no point exists at a location in that population (zero/gap/membership) [S1][S3].  
- What Basis does not govern: if a point does exist, the meaning of an absent value at that point. That is the measure’s fill rule Φ — zero, unknown, or undefined — declared once on the measure and used consistently at every anchor [S5].

Where it lives and how it is used:

- Basis is part of the UNIVERSE declaration (UNIVERSE … BASIS …). Universes are Manifold-level named objects; columns bind to them with ON, and co-universality is checked by reference to the same named universe [S1][S2].  
- Declaring an events projection that is already derivable from a column’s own grain is rejected; the events(...) form exists to name a reusable projection so multiple columns can be co-universal by reference [S2].

Governance note: the basis choice (e.g., “transactions are events; absence = nothing happened” or “inventory is a spine; absence = gap”) is recorded as a claim and marked untestable — data cannot prove what a missing row means; the system keeps that assertion on the record with its verdict [S4].

Citations:  
- Plain-language definition and the zero/gap/membership examples [S3].  
- The four basis forms and how universes are declared and bound [S1][S2].  
- The boundary with fill rule Φ (absence at existing points) [S5].  
- Basis claims are recorded and untestable (verdicts) [S4].
